simple: the rule that stops the experiment by itself when it hurts too much.
analogy: the drill ends the moment anyone actually smells smoke.
precise: a pre-agreed, automatically evaluated condition on the steady-state metric (for example success below 95 % in a 10 s window) that removes the fault and ends the experiment without waiting for a human judgement.
source: R1 of F5-43 (university/labs/F5-43/chaos.log: Listing 1, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0) — a run log of this build

simple: how much can go wrong if the experiment goes badly.
analogy: a drill for one class, or for the whole school.
precise: the share of users, requests, machines or data that an experiment can affect; experiments start with the smallest radius that can disprove the hypothesis and grow only as confidence grows.
source: D10 of F5-43 (Ali Basiri, Niosha Behnam, Ruud de Rooij, Lorin Hochstein, Luke Kosewski, Justin Reynolds, Casey Rosenthal, "Chaos Engineering", IEEE Software (2016) (tier 2; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how fast the allowance is being used compared with spending it evenly.
analogy: using four letters of the allowance in a day when one a day would last exactly the month is a burn rate of four.
precise: the observed bad-event ratio over a window divided by the ratio the SLO allows (1 − SLO); a burn rate of 1 sustained for the whole SLO window consumes exactly the budget, a burn rate of b consumes it in 1/b of the window.
source: D8 of F5-42 (Betsy Beyer, Niall Richard Murphy, David K. Rensin, Kent Kawahara, Stephen Thorne (eds.), "The Site Reliability Workbook" (tier 3; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many different time series a metric turns into.
analogy: one tally column per town is fine; one column per letter-writer's name fills the fridge.
precise: the number of distinct label-value combinations of a metric; each combination is a separate time series that must be stored and queried, so labels with many values (user ids, keys) multiply storage and query cost.
source: R1 of F5-41 (university/labs/F5-41/service.log: Listing 1, g++ (Ubuntu 13.3.0-6ubuntu2~24.04.1) 13.3.0, Linux x86_64 cloud build container, exit code 0) — a run log of this build

simple: a fault-injection test written like a science experiment: say what "normal" looks like, predict it stays normal, break something, measure.
analogy: "during the drill, every letter still arrives within a week".
precise: an experiment that defines the system's steady state by a measurable output (for example the SLI of F5-42), hypothesises that it continues in the experimental group while a real-world event is injected, and tries to disprove the hypothesis by comparison with a control.
source: D10 of F5-43 (Ali Basiri, Niosha Behnam, Ruud de Rooij, Lorin Hochstein, Luke Kosewski, Justin Reynolds, Casey Rosenthal, "Chaos Engineering", IEEE Software (2016) (tier 2; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a file is cut into pieces of equal size; the computers that store the pieces are chunk servers.
analogy: volumes of a long book; a friend's bookshelf.
precise: GFS divides each file into fixed-size chunks, each identified by a chunk handle assigned by the master; chunk servers store chunks as files on their local disks and serve reads and writes of byte ranges.
source: D2 of F5-39 (Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff, Shun-Tak Leung, "The Google File System" (SOSP 2003; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an edition number for each piece, raised whenever writing starts again.
analogy: the edition number on each catalogue card.
precise: a counter kept by the master for each chunk and recorded by its replicas; the master increases it when it grants a new lease, so a replica that was unavailable during that grant keeps an older number and is recognised as stale.
source: D2 of F5-39 (Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff, Shun-Tak Leung, "The Google File System" (SOSP 2003; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: put both keys and computers on a circle of numbers; each key belongs to the next computer round the circle.
analogy: the wheel of letters, each friend owning the stretch before her mark.
precise: a partitioning scheme in which a hash function maps keys and nodes onto the same circular space and each key is assigned to the first node clockwise from its position, so that adding or removing a node moves only the keys of the neighbouring range.
source: D7 of F5-40 (David Karger, Eric Lehman, Tom Leighton, Rina Panigrahy, Matthew Levine, Daniel Lewin, "Consistent Hashing and Random Trees: Distributed Caching Protocols for Relieving Hot Spots on the World Wide Web" (STOC 1997; tier 5; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes)); D4 of F5-40 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: run the work where the data already is.
analogy: the friend with the volume on her shelf counts its words; nobody posts the book.
precise: scheduling a task on (or near) a machine that stores a replica of its input, so the input is read from a local disk instead of over the network.
source: D3 of F5-39 (Jeffrey Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, "MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters" (OSDI 2004; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: one big file system whose files are spread over many computers.
analogy: the club's library spread over five friends' shelves, with one catalogue.
precise: a file system whose namespace and data are stored on multiple networked machines and accessed by clients through a protocol, usually with data replicated across machines so that files survive machine failures.
source: D1 of F5-39 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)); D2 of F5-39 (Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff, Shun-Tak Leung, "The Google File System" (SOSP 2003; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: how many failures the target still allows.
analogy: the allowance card: 30 late letters this month.
precise: one minus the SLO, applied to the window: the number (or fraction) of bad events the service may have in the window while still meeting its SLO; spending it on releases, experiments and incidents is a decision the SLO makes explicit.
source: D5 of F5-42 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: breaking something on purpose to see what happens.
analogy: Leila pretending to be ill for an afternoon.
precise: deliberately introducing failures (process crashes, refused connections, delays, packet loss, disk errors, clock skew) into a system or its environment to test its behaviour under those failures.
source: D10 of F5-43 (Ali Basiri, Niosha Behnam, Ruud de Rooij, Lorin Hochstein, Luke Kosewski, Justin Reynolds, Casey Rosenthal, "Chaos Engineering", IEEE Software (2016) (tier 2; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a scheduled day when a team practises a failure on a real system, together.
analogy: the club's announced fire drill.
precise: a planned exercise in which engineers inject one or more faults into a staging or production system while observing it, to test both the system and the people and procedures that respond.
source: D8 of F5-43 (Betsy Beyer, Niall Richard Murphy, David K. Rensin, Kent Kawahara, Stephen Thorne (eds.), "The Site Reliability Workbook" (tier 3; proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a storage service where you save a value under a name (the key) and get it back by that name.
analogy: the club's address book: look up a name, read the entry.
precise: a data store whose interface is essentially get(key) and put(key, value) on opaque values, without queries across keys; distributed key-value stores partition the key space across nodes and replicate each key.
source: D1 of F5-40 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)); D4 of F5-40 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a time-limited permission for one copy to decide the order of changes.
analogy: Ines tells Kofi "for the next hour, you decide the order of corrections to volume 3".
precise: a grant from the master to one replica of a chunk, the primary, for a limited time; the primary assigns a serial order to all mutations of the chunk, and the secondaries apply them in that order.
source: D2 of F5-39 (Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff, Shun-Tak Leung, "The Google File System" (SOSP 2003; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a way to run one calculation over a huge data set on many computers by writing just two small functions.
analogy: every friend counts the words in the volumes on her own shelf (map), then the counts are sorted by first letter and added up by one friend per letter (reduce).
precise: a programming model and runtime in which a user-supplied map function turns input records into intermediate key/value pairs and a reduce function merges all values of each key; the runtime partitions the work, schedules it on a cluster, and handles failures by re-executing tasks.
source: D3 of F5-39 (Jeffrey Dean, Sanjay Ghemawat, "MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters" (OSDI 2004; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the computer that knows where every piece of every file is.
analogy: Ines and her catalogue card box.
precise: in GFS, the single server that holds the file and chunk namespace, the mapping from files to chunks and the current locations of each chunk's replicas, grants leases and directs re-replication; file data never passes through it.
source: D2 of F5-39 (Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff, Shun-Tak Leung, "The Google File System" (SOSP 2003; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a broken state that keeps itself going after the thing that caused it is gone.
analogy: the post stays jammed after Leila is better, because everyone keeps resending.
precise: a failure in which a trigger pushes a system from a stable good state into a stable bad state, sustained by a feedback effect (typically retries or work amplification) rather than by the trigger; recovery requires removing the sustaining effect, often by shedding load.
source: D11 of F5-43 (Nathan Bronson, Abutalib Aghayev, Aleksey Charapko, Timothy Zhu, "Metastable Failures in Distributed Systems", HotOS (2021) (tier 2; proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: numbers sampled over time: a count that only grows, a value that goes up and down, or counts per range of values.
analogy: the tally sheet on the fridge.
precise: a numeric time series identified by a name and labels; a counter is monotonically increasing (rates are computed from its differences), a gauge is a current value, and a histogram counts observations into fixed buckets so that distributions can be aggregated across instances and time.
source: D5 of F5-41 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: an alert that checks a long and a short window together, so it fires for real trouble and stops soon after it ends.
analogy: ring the bell if the allowance shrank fast over the last day and is still shrinking over the last hour.
precise: an alert condition that requires the burn rate to exceed a threshold over a long window (for significance) and over a short window (so the alert resets quickly after recovery); several such pairs with different thresholds separate urgent pages from tickets.
source: D8 of F5-42 (Betsy Beyer, Niall Richard Murphy, David K. Rensin, Kent Kawahara, Stephen Thorne (eds.), "The Site Reliability Workbook" (tier 3; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: being able to find out what is happening inside a running system from the records it produces.
analogy: the club's diaries, tally sheets and tracking slips together.
precise: the property of a system that its internal state and behaviour can be inferred from its external outputs (telemetry such as logs, metrics and traces), including for questions that were not anticipated when it was built; monitoring is the practice of collecting and acting on such telemetry.
source: D5 of F5-41 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a page wakes someone now; a ticket is a task for working hours.
analogy: ringing the bell at night versus writing a note on the fridge.
precise: the two urgencies of alert notifications: a page requires immediate human action, a ticket requires action within days; an alert that needs no human action should be neither.
source: D5 of F5-42 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the value below which a given share of measurements falls; p99 is "99 of 100 requests were at least this fast".
analogy: line up all letters by delay; the one at position 99 of every 100 is the p99 letter.
precise: the q-quantile of a distribution: the smallest value v such that a fraction q of observations is ≤ v; high percentiles describe the tail that averages hide.
source: D5 of F5-41 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)); D9 of F5-41 (Jeffrey Dean, Luiz André Barroso, "The Tail at Scale" (Communications of the ACM; tier 5; proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the computers that should keep copies of a key, in order.
analogy: the owner of the stretch and the next two friends round the wheel.
precise: in Dynamo, the list of nodes responsible for a key: the first N distinct physical nodes found walking clockwise from the key's position, skipping further virtual nodes of a node already listed.
source: D4 of F5-40 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: keep N copies; wait for W of them on a write and ask R of them on a read.
analogy: write the entry in three books, wait until two friends confirm; when reading, ask two friends and trust the newer entry.
precise: a replication configuration in which a write succeeds after W of the N replicas acknowledge and a read returns after R replicas reply; if R + W > N, every read set intersects every write set, so a read sees at least one replica with the latest successful write (absent sloppy quorums and concurrent writes).
source: D1 of F5-40 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)); D4 of F5-40 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: making a new copy when one copy is lost.
analogy: Ines asks Ravi to photocopy volume 3 for Tomas when Mei's house floods.
precise: the master's action of copying a chunk from a live replica to another chunk server when the number of available replicas falls below the replication target.
source: D2 of F5-39 (Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff, Shun-Tak Leung, "The Google File System" (SOSP 2003; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: "add this record at the end, wherever the end is", done safely by many writers at once.
analogy: several friends posting new reviews to be glued in at the back of the volume, in whatever order they arrive.
precise: a GFS operation in which the client supplies only the data; the primary chooses the offset, and the record is written atomically at least once, so retries after failures may leave duplicate records or padding that readers must skip.
source: D2 of F5-39 (Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff, Shun-Tak Leung, "The Google File System" (SOSP 2003; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a cap on how many retries a client may send, as a share of its normal requests.
analogy: each sender may resend at most one letter in ten.
precise: a limit on retries relative to first attempts (for example retries ≤ 10 % of requests over a window), so that retries help with occasional failures but cannot multiply load during a widespread one.
source: D5 of F5-43 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: failed requests are sent again, which adds load, which makes more requests fail.
analogy: every sender resending each late letter three times, to anyone.
precise: a positive feedback loop in which client or intermediate retries multiply the offered load on a degraded service; amplification is the number of attempts per original request, which can reach the product of the retry limits of every layer.
source: D5 of F5-43 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: keeping only some traces, decided either at the start or at the end of a request.
analogy: clipping slips to every tenth letter, or keeping the slips only of letters that turned out slow.
precise: recording a subset of traces to bound cost; head-based sampling decides when the root span starts (cheap, but blind to the outcome), tail-based sampling buffers spans and decides after the request completes (can keep all slow or failed requests, at the cost of buffering).
source: D7 of F5-41 (Benjamin H. Sigelman et al., "Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure" (Google technical report; tier 5; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: two versions of the same entry that were written without knowing about each other.
analogy: Leila's packing list and Hiro's packing list from the afternoon the line was down.
precise: concurrent versions of one key that the store keeps side by side and returns together on a read, leaving reconciliation to the application.
source: D4 of F5-40 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a promise to customers with consequences if it is broken.
analogy: the club promising members a refund of their stamps if it misses the target.
precise: an explicit or implicit contract with users that includes consequences (often financial) of meeting or missing the SLOs it contains; internal SLOs are normally stricter than any SLA.
source: D5 of F5-42 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a number that measures how well the service is doing for its users.
analogy: the share of letters answered within a week.
precise: a carefully defined quantitative measure of some aspect of the level of service provided, usually a ratio of good events to valid events (for example requests answered without a server error, or requests answered within 100 ms), with the point of measurement stated.
source: D5 of F5-42 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: the target for an SLI over a period.
analogy: "999 of every 1,000 letters within a week, each month".
precise: a target value or range for an SLI measured over a stated time window, for example 99.9 % of requests successful over 30 days.
source: D5 of F5-42 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: if the usual keepers are unreachable, a stand-in keeps the copy and hands it back later.
analogy: Kofi keeps Mei's copy of an entry, with a note "belongs to Mei", while her line is down.
precise: a quorum counted over the first N reachable nodes of the extended preference list rather than over the N home nodes; a stand-in node stores the write with a hint naming the intended node and forwards it when that node is reachable again.
source: D4 of F5-40 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5)); D1 of F5-40 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a copy that missed some changes.
analogy: Mei's volume 3 after her week away.
precise: a replica whose version is older than the master's current version for that chunk; the master excludes it from the locations it gives to clients and removes it later.
source: D2 of F5-39 (Sanjay Ghemawat, Howard Gobioff, Shun-Tak Leung, "The Google File System" (SOSP 2003; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a moment when a whole program stops doing its normal work.
analogy: Arjun reorganising his filing cabinet while nothing else in his house moves.
precise: an interval during which all application threads of a process are suspended, for example by a garbage collector or by a maintenance task holding a global lock; every operation in progress in that process is delayed by the length of the pause.
source: D9 of F5-41 (Jeffrey Dean, Luiz André Barroso, "The Tail at Scale" (Communications of the ACM; tier 5; proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a diary line written as named fields, so a program can read it.
analogy: each diary line has the same boxes: date, letter, from whom, how long.
precise: a timestamped record of a discrete event emitted by a program, with machine-parseable key-value fields (for example level, node, trace, dur_ms) rather than free text, so that events can be filtered, joined and counted.
source: D5 of F5-41 (Betsy Beyer, Chris Jones, Jennifer Petoff, Niall Richard Murphy (eds.), "Site Reliability Engineering" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a note that says "this was deleted", kept instead of just erasing.
analogy: crossing out the stove and writing "removed by Leila" instead of tearing out the line.
precise: a marker stored in place of a deleted item or value so that the deletion can be merged with concurrent versions and propagated to replicas instead of being undone by them.
source: D1 of F5-40 (Martin Kleppmann, "Designing Data-Intensive Applications" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)); D8 of F5-40 (Marc Shapiro, Nuno Preguiça, Carlos Baquero, Marek Zawirski, "Conflict-free Replicated Data Types" (tier 5; proposed in DS301's notes as well)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a trace is the story of one request through all the computers it visited; each step is a span.
analogy: the tracking slip stamped at every post office and every house.
precise: a trace is a tree of spans sharing a trace identifier; a span records one timed operation (name, start, duration, node) with its own identifier and its parent's identifier, so that the causal structure and timing of a request can be reconstructed across processes.
source: D7 of F5-41 (Benjamin H. Sigelman et al., "Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure" (Google technical report; tier 5; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: passing the tracking number along with the request.
analogy: the slip travels clipped to the letter.
precise: carrying the trace identifier and the current span identifier in every request a service sends (for example in RPC metadata), so that the receiver's spans become children of the sender's span.
source: D7 of F5-41 (Benjamin H. Sigelman et al., "Dapper, a Large-Scale Distributed Systems Tracing Infrastructure" (Google technical report; tier 5; not in the guide's F5 registry, proposed in this course's notes)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: a small list of counters, one per writer, that shows which versions came before which.
analogy: each friend numbers her own changes; a version carries the latest number it has seen from each friend.
precise: a map from node identifiers to counters attached to a version; version a descends from version b if every counter of a is greater than or equal to the matching counter of b; if neither descends from the other, the versions are concurrent.
source: D4 of F5-40 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5)); D6 of F5-40 (Maarten van Steen, Andrew S. Tanenbaum, "Distributed Systems" (tier 3; edition to be recorded)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)

simple: each computer puts many marks on the circle instead of one.
analogy: Yara draws many small marks round the wheel, so she takes a few names from everyone.
precise: one of several positions on the ring assigned to the same physical node, which evens out the load and spreads the work of a joining or leaving node over many others.
source: D4 of F5-40 (Giuseppe DeCandia et al., "Dynamo: Amazon's Highly Available Key-value Store" (SOSP 2007; tier 5)) — pending verification (dossier gate G1 open)
